lessons.title: querer — "to want," and the e becomes ie crack again
lessons.gloss: to want (and to love) — a stem-changing verb, e becomes ie

segments.text: Back in Chapter 8, tener cracked its stem: tienes, with the vowel breaking e becomes ie. That wasn't a one-off — it's a whole class of Spanish verbs. Here's the most useful of them: querer, "to want" (and, of a person, "to love").
diphthong-ie — the stem breaks to -ie- under stress: quiero = KYE-ro.
querer comes from Latin quaerere, "to seek, to ask, to want." Seeking and wanting are the same impulse at the root — and that root is a treasure-house of English:
query, quest, question — a seeking.
with prefixes: inquire (in- "into"), require (re- "back"), acquire (ad- "toward"), conquer (con- "thoroughly seek/win"), exquisite ("sought out"), quorum ("of whom" the seeking needs enough).
So when you say quiero, you're using the same "seek" root as question and conquer.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the e becomes ie stem-change (the "boot")

segments.text: querer is a stem-changing verb: when the stem vowel e is stressed, it breaks to ie — exactly the pattern tener showed you.

utterances: yo, quiero, (e becomes ie).
tú, quieres, (e becomes ie).
él/ella/usted, quiere, (e becomes ie).
nosotros, queremos, (plain e — unstressed).
ellos/ustedes, quieren, (e becomes ie).

segments.text: Only queremos keeps the plain e, because there the stress falls on the ending, not the stem. Shade in the forms that change — yo/tú/él…/ellos — and they draw a boot shape around the nosotros/vosotros gap. That "boot" is the signature of every stem-changer.

segments.text: What Latin verb is querer from, and two English cousins? (quaerere "to seek"; query/quest/conquer.) Give its five present forms. (Quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, quieren.) Which form keeps the plain e, and why? (Queremos — the stress is on the ending, not the stem.) Next: poder, with a different crack, o becomes ue.

lessons.title: poder — "to be able," and the o becomes ue crack
lessons.gloss: to be able / can — a stem-changing verb, o becomes ue

segments.text: querer broke e becomes ie. Now meet the other stem-change: o becomes ue. The verb is poder, "to be able / can" — and once you have querer (want) and poder (can), you can say almost anything you want to or can do.
diphthong-ue — the stem breaks to -ue- under stress: puedo = PWE-do (a w-glide).
poder comes from Latin potēre (from posse), "to be able, to have power." It's literally the verb power — and the family shows it:
power itself (English took it through Old French poeir from potēre).
potent, potential, omnipotent ("all-powerful"), possible ("able to be"), posse ("(those) able" to be summoned).
So puedo and power are the same word — one a Spanish verb, the other its English noun.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the o becomes ue stem-change

segments.text: poder is a stem-changer of the o becomes ue kind: the stressed stem o breaks to ue, in the same boot shape (all forms but nosotros/vosotros):

utterances: yo, puedo, (o becomes ue).
tú, puedes, (o becomes ue).
él/ella/usted, puede, (o becomes ue).
nosotros, podemos, (plain o — unstressed).
ellos/ustedes, pueden, (o becomes ue).

segments.text: Just like querer, only podemos keeps the plain vowel. (Other o becomes ue verbs you'll meet: dormir "sleep" becomes duermo, volver "return" becomes vuelvo.)
Point poder at an infinitive to say what you're able to do — just like ir a.
infinitive, but for ability:
Puedo hablar español. — "I can speak Spanish." ¿Puedes venir? — "Can you come?" No puedo — "I can't."

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "poder" then "puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, pueden" — the *ue* crack]

segments.text: What Latin verb is poder from, and its English twin? (potēre "to be able"; power.) Give its five forms. (Puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, pueden.) How do you say "I can speak"? (Puedo hablar — poder + infinitive.) Next: the two cracks (e becomes ie and o becomes ue) side by side.

lessons.title: e becomes ie and o becomes ue — one rule, two vowels
lessons.gloss: the stem-change patterns, side by side — the "boot"

segments.text: You've now seen both stem-changes: querer becomes quiero (e becomes ie) and poder becomes puedo (o becomes ue). They aren't two random quirks — they're one sound-law, and knowing it turns a "memorize each verb" chore into a pattern you can predict.

blocks.title: The rule: stressed short vowels broke

segments.text: In the leap from Latin to Spanish, a short, stressed e broke into ie, and a short, stressed o broke into ue. It happened in ordinary nouns too, not just verbs:

utterances: Latin: terra. Spanish: tierra ("earth"). break: e becomes ie.
Latin: septem. Spanish: siete ("seven"). break: e becomes ie.
Latin: porta. Spanish: puerta ("door"). break: o becomes ue.
Latin: novem. Spanish: nueve ("nine"). break: o becomes ue.

segments.text: (You already met siete and nueve in the numbers — now you know why they have that glide.) In verbs, the stem vowel is stressed in the "boot" forms and unstressed in nosotros/vosotros — so it breaks in the boot and stays plain outside it.

utterances: yo. e becomes ie (querer): quiero. o becomes ue (poder): puedo.
tú. e becomes ie (querer): quieres. o becomes ue (poder): puedes.
él/ella/ud. e becomes ie (querer): quiere. o becomes ue (poder): puede.
nosotros. e becomes ie (querer): queremos. o becomes ue (poder): podemos.
ellos/uds. e becomes ie (querer): quieren. o becomes ue (poder): pueden.

segments.text: Same shape both times: the four "corner" forms crack, the nosotros form stays plain — the boot. tener ( becomes tienes), from Chapter 8, was your first taste; now you own the whole rule.

segments.text: What single sound-law lies behind e becomes ie and o becomes ue? (Short stressed Latin e and o broke into ie and ue.) Which persons crack, and which stays plain? (The "boot" — all but nosotros/vosotros.) Give a noun that shows each break. (tierra from terra; puerta from porta.) Next: nuestro — "our."

lessons.title: nuestro — "our," the possessive that agrees fully
lessons.gloss: our (and vuestro, "your"-plural) — the possessive that agrees fully

segments.text: In Chapter 10 you met mi/tu/su — possessives that change only for number (mis, tus, sus). nuestro ("our") is different: it agrees in both gender and number, like an ordinary -o/-a adjective. It's the fullest-flexing of the possessives.

nuestro comes from Latin noster, "our." You've heard it without knowing: the Paternoster is the "Our Father," and a nostrum is literally "our thing" (a quack's secret remedy). Its partner vuestro ("your," to a group) is from voster/vester.
Notice the stem-change fossil: noster becomes nuestro shows the same o becomes ue break you just learned (short stressed o becomes ue). The possessive cracks exactly like puerta and puedo.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: four forms, agreeing like -o/-a

segments.text: Where mi had two forms (mi/mis), nuestro has four — masculine/feminine × singular/plural:

utterances: masc. singular: nuestro libro. plural: nuestros libros.
fem. singular: nuestra casa. plural: nuestras casas.

segments.text: So it's nuestro coche ("our car," masc.) but nuestra casa ("our house," fem.) — you match the noun in both gender and number, just like bueno/buena/buenos/buenas. vuestro does the same (vuestro/vuestra/vuestros/vuestras).

lessons.title: Practice — querer, poder, and the boot
lessons.gloss: wanting, being able, and the stem-change boot

segments.text: Two power-verbs and a rule this chapter: querer (want, e becomes ie), poder (can, o becomes ue), and the stem-change boot that shapes them both — plus nuestro, the fully-agreeing "our." Drill the cracks until quiero/puedo come without thinking.
querer (e becomes ie): quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, quieren (only queremos stays plain).
poder (o becomes ue): puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, pueden (only podemos stays plain).

blocks.title: Chain the verbs (want to / can + infinitive)

segments.text: Quiero hablar español. — "I want to speak Spanish."
Puedo hablar un poco. — "I can speak a little."
¿Quieres comer? — "Do you want to eat?", ¿Puedes venir? — "Can you come?"
Vamos a poder — "we're going to be able to" (reusing the near future from Ch.10).
nuestra casa (fem.), nuestro coche (masc.), nuestros amigos (masc. pl.) — match gender and number, unlike mi/tu/su.
— ¿Qué quieres hacer? — Quiero ir a un café con nuestros amigos. ¿Puedes venir? — Sí, puedo. Podemos ir ahora.
Every tool of the chapter: quiero (want, e becomes ie), puedes/puedo/podemos (can, o becomes ue), nuestros (our, agreeing), and ir a from Ch.10.
